title: Cost‐effectiveness of a randomized controlled trial comparing low‐dose aspirin to placebo for the prevention of recurrent preterm birth
authors: Anadeijda J E M C Landman
Huib A A M van Vliet
journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics

sections.abstract:
To assess the cost‐effectiveness of low‐dose aspirin compared to placebo for the prevention of recurrent preterm birth from a healthcare perspective. This was a cost‐effectiveness analysis alongside a multicenter, randomized, double‐blinded, placebo‐controlled trial. We included women with a singleton pregnancy and a previous spontaneous preterm birth <37 weeks of gestation of a singleton. Women were randomized between aspirin 80 mg daily and placebo, initiated between 8 and 16 weeks of gestation. We estimated the difference in preterm births (<37 weeks of gestation), and maternal and neonatal healthcare costs using seemingly unrelated linear regression analyses. Bootstrapping was performed to estimate statistical uncertainty. A total of 387 women were included: 194 in the aspirin group and 193 in the placebo group. We observed a small, statistically non‐significant difference in preterm birth (21.2% vs. 25.4%; risk difference −4.3%; 95% CI: −12.7% to 4.1%) and healthcare costs (mean –€99; 95% CI: –€2385 to €2325) in the aspirin group compared to placebo. The cost‐effectiveness acceptability curve showed that the probability of aspirin being cost‐effective was 54% for a willingness to pay threshold of €0 for one prevented preterm birth and 78% for €50 000 for one prevented preterm birth. Our findings suggest that aspirin is the dominant strategy over placebo for the prevention of preterm birth. However, there was substantial uncertainty around the results and definite conclusions regarding the cost‐effectiveness of aspirin cannot be drawn.

Keywords: acetylsalicylic acid, aspirin, cost‐effectiveness, economic analysis, perinatal outcome, preterm birth
sections.introduction:
Preterm birth accounts for 9% to 12% of all live births worldwide. 1 Complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality of children under the age of five. 2 Surviving preterm born children are at increased risk for several short‐ and long‐term morbidities. 3 , 4

Both short‐ and long‐term care for preterm born children have a large financial impact on the healthcare system as well as families. 4 In 2019, the annual costs related to preterm birth in the Dutch healthcare system amounted €132 million, which equals 63% of all perinatal care expenditures. While lifetime costs associated with preterm birth are considered in this calculation, the majority (94%) of these costs are attributed to hospital care. Productivity losses of parents were not considered. 5 Compared to the €1400 for term births, the costs from birth until discharge or neonatal death rise sharply from €2900 for preterm births at 36 weeks of gestation up to €88 100 for preterm births at 24 weeks of gestation, with the mean costs per preterm birth in the Netherlands being €27 500. 6 In the United States, the long‐term incremental costs of preterm birth are estimated to be €60 000 per infant, rising to as much as €315 000 per infant born before 28 weeks of gestation. 7

Preterm birth can be indicated for maternal or fetal reasons, or have a spontaneous onset. Spontaneous preterm birth has a complex and multifactorial etiology. An increasing body of evidence shows placental malperfusion is an important contributor to spontaneous preterm birth, indicating parallels in pathophysiology between pre‐eclampsia and a subgroup of spontaneous preterm birth may exist. 8 As low‐dose aspirin has been proven effective for the prevention of preterm pre‐eclampsia, it has been suggested low‐dose aspirin may also contribute to the prevention of spontaneous preterm birth. 9 , 10 Secondary analyses in women at risk for pre‐eclampsia have indeed shown lower rates of spontaneous preterm births in women taking aspirin. 11 , 12 Low‐dose aspirin has also been shown to reduce overall preterm birth in nulliparous women in low‐ and middle income countries. 13 The APRIL trial, performed by our study group, evaluated the effect of low‐dose aspirin in a high‐risk population for preterm birth, that is, women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth, and found a trend towards less preterm births in the aspirin group. Neonatal outcomes were comparable between groups. 14 , 15

As the costs of aspirin are almost negligible (approximately €10 per pregnancy), a slight reduction in preterm birth is expected to be cost‐saving and, thus, cost‐effective. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the cost‐effectiveness of treatment with aspirin 80 mg in comparison with placebo for the prevention of preterm birth in women from the APRIL trial with a previous spontaneous preterm birth from a healthcare perspective.
sections.methods:
We performed a cost‐effectiveness analysis alongside the APRIL trial. This was a multicenter, double‐blind, randomized trial comparing aspirin 80 mg to placebo for the prevention of preterm birth in high‐risk women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth. This study was registered in the Dutch Trial Register (NL5553, NTR5675) on January 22, 2016. The study protocol and main trial results have been published previously. 14 , 15 Study approval was obtained from the Medical Research Ethics Committee from the Amsterdam Medical Center (no. 2015_332) on February 22, 2016. In addition, the study was approved by the boards of all participating centers. Inclusions started May 31, 2016. The study was reported according to the CONSORT guidelines. 16

The APRIL trial included women with a singleton pregnancy who had a previous spontaneous preterm birth of a singleton between 22 and 37 weeks of gestation. After informed consent, participating women were randomized between 80 mg aspirin or placebo. The primary outcome was preterm birth <37 weeks of gestation. Participants and their infants were followed up until 3 months from the expected date of delivery.

The effect measure was a binary variable indicating the occurrence of preterm birth, defined as birth ≥16 and <37 weeks of gestation. Gestational age was determined by first‐trimester ultrasound according to the Dutch national guidelines. 17 Outcome data were recorded in an electronic case report form based on data from hospital records.

Costs included intervention costs, as well as maternal and neonatal costs from randomization until 3 months after the expected date of delivery. In the antepartum and delivery phase, we included data on the use of the intervention (aspirin or placebo), maternal admissions during pregnancy, tocolysis, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, analgesics during labor, mode of delivery, manual placental removal and blood transfusions. In the postpartum phase, we included data on maternal postpartum admissions, neonatal admissions, days of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or neonatal intubation, surfactant use, and the transfer of neonates to centers with more or less specialized care. For each day of maternal or neonatal admission the level of care was registered: home‐monitoring, ward, medium care or intensive care. Gestational age at initiation and cessation of therapy was obtained from participant‐reported medication diaries. Costs were calculated by multiplying utilization rates with standard costs from the Dutch costing manual, 18 unit costs from a previous study by Nijman et al., 19 and tariffs from the Dutch Health Care Institute 20 and the Dutch Healthcare Authority. 21 Tocolysis costs were calculated as a weighted average of medication of first choice in the participating centers as derived from a survey: 56% nifedipine and 44% atosiban. Table 1 presents the prices used and their corresponding sources. All costs are in 2019 prices. Discounting was not required given the time horizon of this study.

Abbreviation: CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure.

We conducted a cost‐effectiveness analysis from the healthcare perspective that related the occurrence of preterm birth to costs. Data were complete except for three entries: the administration of corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity was missing for one woman and tocolysis use was missing for two women who delivered abroad. We imputed these missing values as a random draw from a distribution based on the probability of the use of this medication among preterm births. We used linear regression models to estimate differences in costs between groups for the following cost categories: antepartum admissions, antepartum medication, delivery, postpartum mother, and postpartum child. For the cost‐effectiveness analysis, differences in total costs and effects between the aspirin and placebo treatment groups were estimated using seemingly unrelated regression analyses, which account for the correlation between costs and effects. We calculated the incremental cost‐effectiveness ratio (ICER) by dividing the difference in costs between groups by the difference in effect of the intervention on the incidence of preterm birth.

To estimate statistical uncertainty around cost differences and the ICER, we used bias corrected and accelerated (BCA) bootstrapping with 5000 repetitions. This uncertainty was presented using a cost‐effectiveness plane (CE plane) and cost‐effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC). The CEAC indicates the probability that aspirin is cost‐effective compared to placebo for different willingness to pay (WTP) thresholds. The WTP threshold indicates the maximum amount of money society is willing to pay for a unit of health effect gained – that is, one preterm birth prevented. We performed all analyses in R statistical programming language, version 4.0.2. The P value for statistical significance was 0.05.

We performed two subgroup analyses in line with the effectiveness paper 14 : (1) a subgroup analysis among women with ≥80% adherence to study medication, and (2) a subgroup analysis among women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth <30 +0 weeks of gestation. Medication adherence was determined based on medication diaries and pill counts. 14
sections.results:
Between May 31, 2016 and June 13, 2019, 387 women were enrolled in the trial: a total of 194 in the aspirin group and 193 in the placebo group. A more detailed description of the study population and baseline characteristics has been published previously. 14

We observed a small, but statistically non‐significant decrease in the incidence of preterm birth <37 weeks of gestation in the aspirin group (21.2%) compared to the placebo group (25.4%; risk difference −4.3%; 95% CI: −12.7% to 4.1%).

As shown in Table 2 , the mean costs per patient in the aspirin group (€7076) were slightly lower than in the placebo group (€7175), but this difference was not statistically significant (−€99, 95% CI: –€2385 to €2325). The antenatal costs were €3175 in the aspirin group and €3087 in the placebo group (€88; 95% CI: –€421 to €961). The largest difference in costs was observed for postpartum costs (−€187; 95% CI: –€2283 to €2144), mostly due to reduced costs for neonatal admissions (−€160; 95% CI: –€2301 to €2017). However, these cost differences were not statistically significant.

Costs per category.

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; SE, standard error.

The ICER was –€2334 per preterm birth prevented (Table 3 ). Although the point estimate of the ICER suggests that aspirin is dominant over placebo, the distribution of bootstrapped results revealed substantial uncertainty: 34% of the bootstrapped samples was located in the NE quadrant of the CE plane suggesting that aspirin prevents preterm birth while increasing costs; 50% was located in the SE quadrant where aspirin is dominant over placebo, suggesting aspirin is more effective and less costly; 4% of the results was located in the SW quadrant suggesting an increase in preterm births and a decrease in costs in the aspirin group; and, finally, 12% was located in the NW quadrant where aspirin is dominated by placebo, suggesting aspirin is less effective and more costly than placebo (Figure 1 ). The CEAC showed that the probability of aspirin being cost‐effective in comparison to placebo for a WTP threshold of €0 for one prevented preterm birth was 54%. This probability increased to 70% for a WTP of €20 000, and to 78% for a WTP of €50 000 for one prevented preterm birth (Figure 2 ).

Cost‐effectiveness analysis.

Abbreviations: ICER, incremental cost‐effectiveness ratio; SE, standard error.

For the cost‐effectiveness outcomes, the treatment effect was multiplied by −1 to make the interpretation consistent with readers' expectations.

Cost‐effectiveness plane.

Cost‐effectiveness acceptability curve.

Among women with ≥80% adherence to medication, the preterm birth rate in the aspirin group was −5.6% (95% CI: −15.7% to 4.5%) while the costs were higher (€718, 95% CI: –€1800 to €4032) as compared to placebo, although this was not statistically significant (Table S1 ). The ICER was €12 843 per preterm birth prevented. The CEAC showed the probability of aspirin begin cost‐effective was 31% for a WTP of €0 per prevented preterm birth, 57% for a WTP of €20 000 and 71% for a WTP of €50 000.

The subgroup analysis among women with a previous spontaneous birth <30 +0 weeks of gestation showed a statistically significant preterm birth risk difference of −13.3% (95% CI: −25.9% to −0.1%) with statistically non‐significant higher costs (€567, 95% CI: –€3741 to €5464) (Table S2 ). The ICER was €4253 per prevented preterm birth. The probability of aspirin being cost‐effective in comparison to placebo was 41% for a WTP threshold of €0 per one prevented preterm birth, 74% for a WTP threshold of €20 000, and 89% for a WTP of €50 000.
sections.discussion:
We performed a cost‐effectiveness analysis from a healthcare perspective, alongside an RCT comparing aspirin 80 mg with placebo for the prevention of recurrent preterm birth. We observed a small, statistically non‐significant reduction of 4% in preterm birth while healthcare costs were €99 lower in the aspirin group compared to placebo. The ICER indicates aspirin may be dominant over placebo (i.e., clinically superior and cost‐saving) for the prevention of preterm birth in women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth. However, there is substantial uncertainty around the results, driven by the uncertainty about the effectiveness of aspirin to prevent preterm birth and subsequent neonatal complications. The CEAC shows a 54% probability of the intervention being cost‐effective for a WTP €0 and 70% for a WTP €20 000 per preterm birth prevented.

The strengths of this cost‐effectiveness analysis include its multicenter and randomized design and the complete data on health outcomes. The main limitation is that the trial was underpowered to detect a reduction in preterm birth due to a lower‐than‐expected event rate. Furthermore, the relatively small sample size, particularly the low incidence of early preterm births (at 24 +0 –28 +0 and 28 +1 –34 +0 weeks), makes the data susceptible to variations by chance as demonstrated by the large uncertainty observed around the costs and effect estimates. As the neonatal admissions costs are the main cost drivers, slight variations in proportions of early preterm births between treatment groups quickly skew the data. This might explain the higher costs in the aspirin group that were observed in the subgroup analyses, particularly in the subgroup analysis on good adherence to medication. We did not observe any significant maternal or neonatal harm in the aspirin group which could explain the higher costs. 14

Other limitations are the short time horizon which covered the moment of randomization until 3 months after the expected date of delivery and the lack of data on treatments administered to the neonates other than ventilatory support, surfactant and transportation costs. Finally, our analysis was performed from a healthcare perspective and did not include productivity losses. A societal perspective, including productivity losses, is generally recommended in the Netherlands to allow for the identification of cost shifts between sectors. Considering the comparable short‐term perinatal outcomes in our study, we expect that long‐term outcomes and societal costs may also be comparable between groups.

Low‐dose aspirin has been proven to reduce the rate of overall preterm birth among women at risk of pre‐eclampsia and in nulliparous women. 9 , 13 , 22 Whether there is a place for low‐dose aspirin administration in the prevention of spontaneous preterm birth remains uncertain. Based on the results of the present trial, a beneficial effect in certain subgroups (i.e., women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth <30 weeks of gestation) cannot be excluded. 14 Taken together with the results from other studies showing a possible beneficial effect of low‐dose aspirin for the prevention of spontaneous preterm birth, aspirin is still a promising intervention for this indication. 11 , 12 Perinatal outcome and the costs of preterm birth are strongly inversely correlated to gestational age at preterm birth, and preventing or delaying preterm birth will likely benefit perinatal outcome and reduce costs. 6 If future trials confirm aspirin's clinical effectiveness for the prevention of spontaneous preterm birth, it would be expected to be cost‐effective considering the negligible costs of aspirin (€10 per pregnancy) and a reduction of the high costs associated with preterm birth. Considering the high medical and economic burden of preterm birth, even a small reduction of 4%, as observed in our study, would be of great relevance.

In the subgroup analysis among women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth <30 +0 weeks of gestation, we observed a high probability of aspirin being cost‐effective as compared to placebo. This may be a reflection of varying proportions of different underlying etiologies of spontaneous preterm birth across the gestational age spectrum. A better understanding and clinical recognition of pathophysiologic mechanisms, and a better understanding of the effect of aspirin is needed to target therapy based on etiology, rather than using gestational age cutoffs as a proxy.

There is an ongoing debate on universal aspirin administration during pregnancy for the prevention of preterm pre‐eclampsia. 23 Universal aspirin use would probably improve other pregnancy outcomes related to uteroplacental insufficiency as well, that is, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and perinatal death. 9 , 24 Recent cost‐effectiveness analyses have shown universal aspirin to be the dominant strategy over targeted aspirin use following either history‐based screening strategies or combined biomarker and ultrasound screening measures. These studies showed significant health gains of universal aspirin use, and it was cost‐saving. 25 , 26 However, some concerns about universal aspirin that have been raised are acceptability, compliance, and the safety for mother and child. 23 , 27 Meta‐analyses did not show increased maternal bleedings risk nor any other major harm. 9 , 28 There may be an increased risk of rash or hives. 29 As for the long‐term health of children with antenatal aspirin exposure, there seems to be no harm based on the available literature. 30 , 31

Due to the concerns about universal aspirin use, aspirin prophylaxis following risk‐based first‐trimester screening strategies for pre‐eclampsia is also being advocated. Although screening tests incur additional costs, this targeted approach is still cost‐effective compared to routine care. 26 , 27 , 32 However, prognostic models for spontaneous preterm birth have poor performance as compared to pre‐eclampsia. 33 The prediction of spontaneous preterm birth remains challenging due to its multifactorial etiology.

Alternatively to screening tests, low‐dose aspirin administration to nulliparous women is being considered as nulliparity is an important risk factor for both pre‐eclampsia and preterm birth. 34 , 35 The ASPIRIN trial was the first trial evaluating low‐dose aspirin compared to placebo with preterm birth as the primary outcome and showed a large reduction of preterm birth among nulliparous women in low‐ and middle‐income countries. 13 Their cost‐effectiveness analysis showed aspirin is cost‐effective and resulted in costs of $248 per prevented preterm birth, $471 per prevented perinatal death and $15.95 per disability‐adjusted life year. 36
sections.limitations:
The strengths of this cost‐effectiveness analysis include its multicenter and randomized design and the complete data on health outcomes. The main limitation is that the trial was underpowered to detect a reduction in preterm birth due to a lower‐than‐expected event rate. Furthermore, the relatively small sample size, particularly the low incidence of early preterm births (at 24 +0 –28 +0 and 28 +1 –34 +0 weeks), makes the data susceptible to variations by chance as demonstrated by the large uncertainty observed around the costs and effect estimates. This might explain the higher costs in the aspirin group that were observed in the subgroup analyses, particularly in the subgroup analysis on good adherence to medication. We did not observe any significant maternal or neonatal harm in the aspirin group which could explain the higher costs. 14

Other limitations are the short time horizon which covered the moment of randomization until 3 months after the expected date of delivery and the lack of data on treatments administered to the neonates other than ventilatory support, surfactant and transportation costs. Finally, our analysis was performed from a healthcare perspective and did not include productivity losses. A societal perspective, including productivity losses, is generally recommended in the Netherlands to allow for the identification of cost shifts between sectors. Considering the comparable short‐term perinatal outcomes in our study, we expect that long‐term outcomes and societal costs may also be comparable between groups.
sections.conclusion: Our findings suggest that aspirin is dominant over placebo for the prevention of preterm birth among high‐risk women with a previous spontaneous preterm birth. However, the substantial uncertainty around the results makes the study inconclusive. Consequently, we do not recommend the widespread implementation of aspirin for this indication at this time. We encourage further research on the effect of low‐dose aspirin for the prevention of spontaneous preterm in large placebo‐controlled trials assessing short‐ and long‐term clinical outcomes as well as cost‐effectiveness.
